Thank you, Chair Curtis, and thanks everyone for the opportunity to be here today. I'm just gonna pull up my slides really quickly. Um, I think I know most of you but if not, I'm Missy Stults, the director of our Office of Sustainability and Innovations. And I'm joined tonight by a few of my colleagues who were involved in this franchise discussion. I see Steve Harvey from DTE and Dan Mahoney as well from DTE. Not with us tonight on the negotiating team are Sky Stewart from the City of Ann Arbor, uh, and of course, H.J. Decker from DTE, who played a pivotal role, as well as Valerie Rader. So I just want to give, um, acknowledgments where they're due. So I'm going to run point in kind of walking you through what this thing is, why we did what we did, and then the team is here to help answer any questions that you might have that emerge. So let's do a quick look back. Uh, the way I'm going to do this is I'm going to provide a little bit of context because this is a really underutilized conversation tool, and it's just foreign for most of us. What is a franchise? What does it mean? What does it do? Give you a sense of where we were and a sense of where we're headed, and then, of course, we'll open it up for, for question. So let's start with what a franchise is, and this also illuminates what it's not. So a franchise is a contract between a local unit of government and a utility, and that contract really governs two things: the use of the rights of way, right? And then the second are some conditions under which the company, that utility may, for a period of time, provide that service. Traditionally, these are pretty cut and clear. You give someone the right to use your right of way. They provide fiber. They provide electricity, right? These, these are pretty traditional tools, but importantly it is a contract, so this is a contract negotiation. In Ann Arbor, our heating franchise was last signed in nineteen ninety-seven, and it was a thirty-year franchise set to expire in January of twenty twenty-seven. Now, you know DTE and Ann Arbor both have sustainability goals. So this is the context in which we're sitting. Of course, we've got A2Zero that's guiding us, and we have this opportunity really to think about our franchise. And I just want to pause. There's a different conversation we can have on the electric side. Our electric franchise is non-negotiable. So we... This is not a muscle, number one, that the city has. We don't negotiate these things regularly. Number two, thirty years ago is a really long time. There are no staff that negotiated that franchise that still exist in the city, right? So we had to walk into this and really get skilled up. As we were thinking about this context, we made the decision that we would negotiate, um, and honestly, we negotiated with multiple entities to try to figure out what a heating franchise would look like that moved us closer to our goals. And I want to give credit to DTE for coming to the table w-with ideas. And, uh, you may not like this franchise, but I will tell you it is the best deal of every entity that we talk to. And so we are excited to be here. There's work to be done. There's no doubt about that. Uh, if you know OSI, you know we don't stop just because we have a thing. We've made forward progress, and we all know we have more work to do. But I would be remiss if I didn't say that the DTE ta-team came in good faith with ideas and really helped us struggle with some of these issues. And so fast-forward, uh, to April of... well, Earth Day of last year, and we adopted a ten-year franchise. So we went from a thirty-year kind of standard franchise to this ten-year franchise. It is the first franchise on the heating side in the country that has a climate commitment. I don't think it's worth downplaying that. The first in the country where a gas utility and a municipality negotiated these terms and had these frank conversations. That is, uh, sad and also incredible, right? So we know we're, we're sort of setting ourselves up for more of these conversations. And of course, there is, uh, it's not just a one-time thing. There's a lot in this franchise I'm going to walk through in just a second. So we meet quarterly to talk about how we're doing, where are our pain points, where are there opportunities for expansion. So this isn't just a one-time the team kind of negotiated. We also continue working to figure out how we're going to make this living and continue advancing our shared goals, in particular around sustainable advancements. So that's just a little bit of context. Um, it is very easy to walk into a negotiating room and have every idea you can possibly imagine. It's really quite different when you have to start putting pen to paper and figure out where you can move. And so I think both of us actually, um, had r-really meaningful, thoughtful conversations and moved in this. So our caller mentioned the ARCA, the Agreement Regarding Climate Action. This-- so the franchise itself, there's three documents that go with, uh, what was adopted. We have the franchise, then we have the ARCA, and then we have a work plan. So I'm going to take you... The franchise is the franchise. It basically does those two things I said. It talks about the right to use our space, um, our rights of way for t-ten years, and there are some general terms in it. The ARCA is associated with that franchise. It's actually specifically talked about in the document itself. And here's where we have a, a commitment to support A2Zero, right? This is binding and enforceable. That, that is part of what we negotiated. Another piece of that is that we have this group that meets quarterly, and it's leadership. It is, it is, uh, we bring in other people as needed, but these are people who have the authority to make decisions, and that includes some decisions around spend. So if we come up with other programs or initiatives, we have authorization up into a certain dollar amount to make those decisions. So that committee that meets regularly, uh, includes someone who reports directly to the city administrator on our side, someone who reports directly to DTE Gas in, in, uh, DTE's side, and then we have others. And then I mentioned the work plan, and again, I'll walk through some of that. But this is the living document that chronicles what we're going to do over a two-year period because we needed a sliding timeline to be able to respond to information as we're learning. Some things are falling away because we're getting them done. Uh, some new opportunities are em-emerging, and so this work plan becomes where we can really iterate together. So in the ARCA, we've got this leadership panel that meets quarterly, which we've been doing. We have, as I mentioned, the authority to commit staff time and actual budget to implement the work plan as we've agreed upon. Uh, we-- if we can't agree, we've got a process for what that looks like, including having the city administrator and the president of DTE Gas get together and make the final determination on what we do. Uh, the ARCA can be terminated, but if the ARCA is terminated without agreement between both parties, the city retains its right to revoke the franchise. N-That's-- that is a powerful lever. I don't think anyone wants that lever to be pulled, but that, uh, was important for us in the discussion to make sure we both were really committed to doing this work. And I'm, I am actually really delighted that we are, and so far, at least in our first year, have demonstrated that. So here's what's in the work plan, kind of in buckets. This is the first two-year work plan, right? So now moving on to that third piece of the document. The ARCA governs the structure and now the implementation. So this is where the, the real substance is. For the first two years, of which we're rounding out the first year, we've got commitments around energy waste reduction. In particular, there was a commitment that DTE would pilot an energy waste reduction program, an energy efficiency program in the rental market. This is a really hard-to-tap market segment. Of course, we have Green Rental Housing. We want to help people come into compliance. We want everyone to live in safe, healthy, and affordable units. DTE obviously has EWR goals. This is a nice mutual overlap. We have been working on this actively. We are very close, uh, to launching something, and I'll share that momentarily with you all. Um, this is, this is exciting for me because it's real dollars going into the community, and the five hundred thousand was the floor and not the ceiling. If this is successful... Let me back up. When this is successful, we have agreed to make this a pilot, uh, to bring it before the commission and see if we can scale it throughout the rest of the territory. Uh, just so you know, I'll steal my thunder in the future, OSI is bringing money to this too, because we think we can go really deep, really far and fast together in some of the energy efficiency work we want to do. Uh, this is important because we are seeing that it's hard to deal with the split in- between landlords and renters who makes the investment in efficiency, especially if the, the person who makes the investment isn't the person who pays the utility bills. So we're trying to overcome that. So you can see here, um, we are really close. Uh, we have a goal of launching this program in the next several weeks. So we are in final design. We have been spending hours sequestered figuring out exactly where money goes, what the process looks like, the application flow. So this is actively moving forward. Uh, it likely will come under the name Insulate Ann Arbor because we're gonna focus on insulation. As we found for the Green Rental Housing program, that is the number one thing a rental can do to come into compliance with the ordinance, is just have insulation. And I will stop and let you think about that for a second. That's all they have to do to be in compliance. Uh, another area is geothermal. Uh, we... This one is, is a really interesting landscape because as you know, we're trying to understand geothermal as a viable, sustainable heating source for us. And so in the negotiations, we wanted to make sure that we kept everything competitive. And so the commitment we got from DTE here really was to being involved in the project and competing in a process. It wasn't a unilateral, "You're gonna build a geothermal system for us." That was something we could have explored. We felt like the best path here was to make sure they were, uh, involved broadly and in good faith would submit a bid into the process. And that was of interest to all parties. I think all of us are excited to understand the viability of geothermal, where it's working, where it's not. Um, in particular network geothermal. I don't think we're questioning the viability of geothermal by itself, but network geothermal has different economics. Um, when does it work when you're in a single family residential neighborhood versus a mixed use commercial district? And so there's a lot of learning that can happen in this landscape. And so the commitment was for DTE to be involved in that process, uh, in, in kind of a good faith effort with city maintaining ownership of that infrastructure. So here we are, we're finishing the designs. The m- the first project is Bryant. Um, if we move forward with the second project, they also committed to bid into a second project. And you can see the dollars here. Um, these were kind of best guesses as we were negotiating of what the max capital cost could be for these systems. We are finishing on the city side, the tech specs. Uh, DTE has joined us at meetings we've had with the market. Uh, I've seen Steve and HJ at those meetings where we're talking about the geothermal project in Bryant. And we're asking contractors for input to make sure our contracting process is thoughtful. Uh, we're strategizing about ways to make sure this is the lowest cost possible, but yet a really robust system, and they're actively contributing in that, that process. So I would say completely and totally on track here. Two other areas to talk about. Biodigester. So this was one where we wanted to understand the feasibility. We have a lot of interest in a biodigester at our wastewater treatment plant or our water, uh, recovery facility. We've really wanted this for a long time, and DTE agreed to bring expertise to the table to help us understand the viability. And so very early after we signed the franchise, they brought in some, uh, third-party technical experts. We all sat down. We opened our books. We looked at the economics. We looked at design work that's been done before. Um, we really, really got into this, and they brought a lot of expertise to the table to help us explore it. And we made the decision, this is not gonna move forward at this time. The economics do not look good. It's gonna be a really tough project. So we're gonna... We, we have a lot more skill. We've been skilled up as staff. We're gonna put that in a bike lot for right now, and we're gonna pivot to some other things. So this is an area where the expertise of DTE and their ecosystem really helped us get to decision fast and would've taken us a lot of time and probably a lot of resources allocated to be able to get to where we are. So thank you for that. We have, uh, a commitment in a work plan to adjust transition for workers. And so here it's really helping implement the training plan that we've created for our geothermal project with our trade unions. And then there's an agreement to help fundraise, which they did in fact help fundraise for the DOE award that we have, that ten million dollar award. They wrote letters of support, letters of commitment to that project. Um, where we haven't had progress yet, and this is not because I think any of us don't want progress, it's just we're very busy, and honestly this one fell through my mind, um, if I'm really honest, as we've been working on all the other elements. Uh, DTE agreed to fund, uh, five thousand a year for local, uh, UA 190 as well as one of the Detroit unions to help them skill up their workforce for geothermal, and that can be used for, of course training, geothermal system insulation, et cetera. So, uh, side note, Steve will add this to our work plan for our next quarterly meeting, but this, this is one that we're all agreed. We negotiated it with the unions. We feel really strong about it. Just, uh, an invoice hasn't come yet, right? So we've got to get that, that in process.

Yeah. And, and we, we have, uh, reached out to UA 190. Uh, we just haven't been able to connect to make sure that we're putting this in the right place, supporting the right training programs, those types of things. So trying to get that meeting on the books now, Missy.

Yeah. Thanks, Steve. That's great. That's great. Okay. Um, last few things just to go through. A- we have... This is, this is one that is really interesting for me. Uh, we have a agreement in our work plan around pushing repair versus replacement where we can in the city, with the exception of, of safety, right? If we've got an explosion risk pipe, there's no question we gotta fix that. Just period, no question. But we talked a lot around what does this look like? We know that we wanna move to sustainable heating options. We don't wanna lock in legacy infrastructure. And so we agreed that when DTE was doing a replacement project, they would give us advance notice, and we had a chance to really challenge that and say, "Why? Why? Why?" And that does not mean we can say no. I wanna be explicit. We did not get to that point. But I think let's open up the vulnerability that has. That means we now know as staff Why projects are happening, and sometimes we may not agree with why. And that means I can take that information, and I can add that to rate cases and other-- so other arguments we're making before the Public Service Commission, and that's a really vulnerable place for our utility to be. And so the fact that we even got to this is forward progress, and it's helping us understand why DTE is making the recommendations on capital investments. So I, I don't-- I think this-- I understand why people are upset this doesn't go all the way, but I think it is really worth sitting for a second in how much progress we got on this very topic. We've had a few discussions around this. There have not been many of these projects that have come forward. And then planning coordination. This may feel small as we're a sustainability commission talking about it, but this is really important for lived experience in the city. We wanna get to a dig once approach. If we're tearing up the streets to do a water main project, that's a great time to come in and do repair on gas infrastructure if it's needed. So we're working deeply on alignment around when we're gonna be in the streets, when DTE needs to be in the streets to repair something, to see if we can pull projects forward or if they can pull projects forward. So the lived experience of our residents is not one of my street is always torn up. It is nope, it is done, uh, the projects are all coordinated. It is much more seamless of an experience, and then my road is nice and good to go. So this, we've been having separate quarterly check-in meetings where we're talking about our capital projects. We've even seen DTE pull projects forward to align with us already. So this is brand new. Again, we're in the first few months of the franchise, but we are seeing that coordination which I think will cascade into a better lived experience for our residents. And then, uh, data and making sure that we have alignment. Um, for the sustainability office, we obviously do a lot of reporting, right? Our greenhouse gas reporting, we have our benchmarking ordinances. And so it's making sure that we can get the data that we need need in a timely way, and there's, there's always work to be done on this. So last slide here on the work plan. Two other areas, infrastructure repairs. We had some, uh, we had some issues that we sort of identified where infrastructure, it wasn't clear how city infrastructure had been damaged. DTE looked at that and said, "Yep, some of this is ours. Nope, it's not ours." Uh, but anything that they identified as, and we probably did that, they have stepped forward and made repairs and coordination is underway on it. So that's been, um, maybe seems like a small pain point, but this does happen, right? You're drilling in the ground, you can't see things, so it's powerful. And then the last area's around customer service, making sure people can get good information when they need it, whether that's for benchmarking or they have a challenging situation going on with their, their gas. And so we are checking in regularly as, as issues emerge and come to our attention, and we're working on processes to make sure both of us want our, everyone to have a really good customer service experience, whether they're working with the city or they're working with DTE. So we have work to do in this area, but it's an area that we openly and actively talked about, and continue to talk about. So just to kind of conclude, let me give you a look forward. We are, in the next few months, gonna be launching Insulate Ann Arbor. Real dollars, right, going out to our community. We are gonna focus... It- I said Insulate 'cause that's the name we're gonna go for, but it's insulation and air sealing. That's just not as beautiful as Insulate Ann Arbor. So Insulate is what it's gonna be called. Uh, we will continue to do our coordinating meetings. We are making progress on data access and transparency. Always work to be done here, I think, on both of our sides, so we're really doubling down on that. And we will start very soon thinking about what's in our next two-year work plan. You just heard Steve mention our work with the unions and helping with the just transition, so that's kind of, like, the, the next real tangible action that you're gonna see movement on. And then we are as a city, based on this process, we've identified DTE's energy manager program, and we will almost certainly be bringing someone in to help us identify more energy-saving opportunities. Because I didn't talk about this in the work plan, but one of the things DTE agreed to was to help us figure out how to decarbonize city buildings. And so this is an area where we can really leverage the expertise to think about things like we're gonna have a boiler that goes out. How do we get ahead of that and make sure we're thinking about obviously efficiency, but the right transition for a very large piece of infrastructure? So this was a lot, uh, but I wanted to make sure we at least had some framing about what the franchise is, what it's not, what we're working on. Um, and I think like any relationship, it continues to evolve and grow. And as I close, I just wanna offer gratitude for everyone in the public who's given us feedback. And I know sometimes in Ann Arbor it's hard to say this, but I need to be explicit. I wanna give gratitude to DTE for these conversations. The sincerity which they showed up into a room with a whole bunch of people, all women, uh, ready to negotiate and go hard at our goals and our values. And they didn't just receive it, they, they authentically engaged in that conversation. So the future, we've got a lot to do, but I think we have the right catalytic players in the room to do something that no one has done before. Steve, Dan, is there anything you wanna add?

Uh, I just wanna thank you, Missy. Um, no, I agree. I think this is a great opportunity for us to move this forward together. Uh, and the city's been a fantastic partner for DTE, giving us the opportunity to learn as well and figure out what the future looks like. Um, looking forward to, to continuing this work and continuing to provide for the city. I'm an Ann Arbor resident, so, um, I, I reap the benefits of, of all these great o- things we have going on in the city as well. So, um, appreciate it. Thank you. Yeah.

uh, in terms of uptake. Um, perhaps that's not- still the case. I know, you know, things have been getting more popular with energy efficiency and stuff. So we have everyone is gonna get-- in-interact with us at least every three years, some of them every two and a half years. In addition, we've been working with the Washtenaw Area Apartment Association, Tenant Association, and others to make sure they're aware of this program is coming. And so we will, uh, be able to, to hopefully get high adoption quickly. Um, we internally are talking about what happens if the money goes really fast.
